solutions.check: 31 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: see 28ac.
President, despot — no balls-up put off

indicators.note: a balls-up is British slang for a mess or botched job, so these letters are made a mess of

explanation.surface: A president and a despot agree there must be no blunder, so they delay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'balls-up' scrambles DESPOT and NO into OSTPONED, after P. A balls-up is a British slang term for a blunder.
explanation.definitionFit: To postpone something is to defer it to a later time, which is what put off means.

clue.text: Let Nigel finally moderate

indicators.note: takes the final letter of Nigel

explanation.surface: A plea to allow Nigel (Farage, presumably) to tone things down at last.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Let' reads as a command opening the sentence; it is the definition, as in 'let a flat'.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the property sense: landlords let or lease a flat to a tenant.

clue.text: Naturally, welcoming Fed chief is probably not Trump's preferred situation

indicators.note: welcoming means taking in a guest, so the phrase for naturally takes a letter inside it

parts.note: of course means naturally, as in 'naturally, I agree'

indicators.note: chief means head or first, so only the first letter of Fed is used

parts.note: the word Fed, whose first letter is taken

explanation.surface: Of course, letting in the Federal Reserve chair is hardly what Trump wants.
explanation.walkthrough: 'chief' takes F from Fed, and 'welcoming' puts it inside OF COURSE after the OF. The definition jokes about Trump's love of golf: a ball off course is where a golfer does not want to be.
explanation.definitionFit: Being off course means straying from the fairway or route, a golfer's nightmare.

clue.text: Fake news ending, "contained in strong beer"

parts.note: F is forte, the musical direction for loud or strong

indicators.note: contained in means held within, so the letter goes inside the word for beer

parts.note: ale is a kind of beer

indicators.note: ending means the last letter, so only the final letter of news is used

parts.note: the word news, whose last letter is taken

explanation.surface: A jibe about fake news, as if its last line were found in a pint of strong beer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ending' takes S from news and 'contained in' puts it inside ALE, making ALSE, after F for forte.
explanation.definitionFit: False and fake both mean untrue or not genuine, as in false teeth or fake news.

clue.text: OBN candidate, babe who wants to go places?

definitions.meaning: a sycophant, fit for Private Eye's Order of the Brown Nose

definitions.text: babe who wants to go places?
definitions.meaning: a baby on all fours, on the move

explanation.surface: An ambitious young thing angling for honours by flattering the powerful.
explanation.walkthrough: OBN is Private Eye's mock honour, the Order of the Brown Nose, given to shameless flatterers. 'Wants to go places' sounds like ambition, but the babe is a baby learning to move.
explanation.definitionFit: A crawler is a toady who sucks up, and also a baby that has started crawling.

clue.text: Out-and-out Trump subordinate heading off comment

parts.note: VANCE, the US Vice President, without the V

explanation.surface: A complete Trump underling heading off to avoid giving a comment.
explanation.walkthrough: JD Vance is Trump's Vice President, so he is the subordinate who loses his head.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: any remark spoken aloud counts as an utterance.

clue.text: Jagger's cosying up to Blair?

definitions.note: Jagger is a Stone, one of the Rolling Stones, rather than a synonym for the word.

indicators.note: the S snuggles right next to the following piece

explanation.surface: Mick Jagger getting friendly with Tony Blair.
explanation.walkthrough: Tony Blair was often matily called 'Tone'; the apostrophe S is lifted straight from 'Jagger's' and set beside him.
explanation.definitionFit: Mick Jagger is a Stone, frontman of the Rolling Stones.

clue.text: Society in old Elizabeth I's rule

parts.note: first letter of BESS, which will hold the S

explanation.surface: A history note on court society under the reign of Elizabeth I.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rule' looks like the monarch's reign, but it is a verb: to dominate one's thoughts. Elizabeth I was known as Good Queen Bess.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that obsesses you rules your mind.

clue.text: Bust ruptured with nail? Capital!

indicators.note: the letters are broken apart and reformed

explanation.surface: A statue's bust smashed with a nail, greeted with a cry of 'Excellent!'
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital!' reads as an old-fashioned cry of approval. Istanbul was the capital of the Ottoman Empire, which is why the exclamation mark hedges.
explanation.definitionFit: Istanbul was long the capital of the Byzantine and Ottoman empires.

clue.text: Lawsuit makes e.g. Momentum F-off

indicators.note: off means removed, so the letter F is taken away from the group word

parts.note: Momentum is a left-wing faction within the UK Labour Party

explanation.surface: A legal case shows the Momentum group being told to get lost.
explanation.walkthrough: Momentum is a British left-wing campaign group within the Labour Party, an example of a FACTION; 'off' removes its F. 'F-off' doubles as rude slang for go away.
explanation.definitionFit: An action is a legal proceeding brought in court, the same thing as a lawsuit.

clue.text: Patchy article on male "transitional"

parts.note: a piece is an article, as in a newspaper piece

indicators.note: transitional means changing from one state to another, so the letters of male change their order

explanation.surface: A patchy newspaper article about a man who is transitioning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'transitional', in quotes, signals the letters of MALE changing into MEAL, after PIECE.
explanation.definitionFit: Piecemeal means done bit by bit, unevenly, so the result is patchy and incomplete.

clue.text: Key Republican charge is repelled

indicators.note: pushed back, so written backwards

explanation.surface: A vital Republican accusation is fought off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Key' looks like an adjective meaning important, but it is a noun: a low island, as in the Florida Keys.
explanation.definitionFit: A key (or cay) is a low island or reef.

clue.text: God's book hijacked by USA in turmoil

indicators.note: hijacked by means seized and held by, so the letter for book is held inside the jumbled letters
turmoil is confusion and disorder, so the letters of USA and in are mixed up

explanation.surface: A sacred book is commandeered by an America in chaos.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in turmoil' scrambles USA and IN into ANUIS, and 'hijacked by' puts B inside it, after ANU.
explanation.definitionFit: Anubis is the jackal-headed ancient Egyptian deity of the dead and embalming.

clue.text: Support Hunt — make a U-turn

explanation.surface: Politicians urged to back Jeremy Hunt and change course.
explanation.walkthrough: Capital H makes 'Hunt' look like Jeremy Hunt, the Tory politician; it is just the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: a politician's U-turn is reversing course, retracing steps already taken.

clue.text: Title: "Pub Reversed Net Zero"

parts.note: the phrase Net Zero with its two words in reversed order is zero net, written as O for zero followed by net

explanation.surface: A headline announcing that a pub has abandoned its net-zero carbon pledge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reversed' does not turn any letters round: it swaps the order of the two words, so Net Zero becomes zero then net.
explanation.definitionFit: A baronet is a hereditary British rank, so the word is itself a title held by its bearer, Sir someone.

clue.text: Stuck up character after bishop's seat

indicators.note: after means coming later, so the reversed Greek letter is placed following the bishop's letter

parts.note: B is the chess abbreviation for bishop

indicators.note: stuck up means raised, and in a down clue the letters read upwards, i.e. backwards

parts.note: mu is a character, a letter of the Greek alphabet

explanation.surface: A snooty type takes the bishop's throne.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stuck up' looks like snobbery but reverses MU into UM, which goes 'after' B. Bum is British slang for the buttocks.
explanation.definitionFit: Seat is a polite word for the buttocks, which bum names informally.

clue.text: Yank and the flustered Tory leadership contender

parts.note: to yank is to tug, pull sharply

indicators.note: flustered means agitated and confused, so the letters of and plus the are mixed up

explanation.surface: An American and a nervous Conservative hopeful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yank' looks like an American but is the verb, giving TUG; 'flustered' scrambles AND THE into ENDHAT. Tom Tugendhat stood for the British Conservative leadership in 2022 and 2024.
explanation.definitionFit: Tom Tugendhat is a British Conservative MP who ran for leader of the Tory party.

clue.text: Kinky medical spout

indicators.note: something kinky is bent or twisted, so the letters of medical come out bent into a new order

explanation.surface: Some unconventional kit found in a doctor's surgery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spout' looks like a noun, a nozzle on medical equipment; it is the verb, to hold forth.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym with a sneer: to spout is to hold forth pompously, as an orator declaims.

clue.text: American second-rate party guys from which shit originates

explanation.surface: A scathing verdict on a poor-quality American frat party as the source of all the trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition takes 'shit' literally, though the surface uses it as slang for rubbish.
explanation.definitionFit: Faeces are produced in the gut, housed in the abdomen.

clue.text: Medic on the brink — look for a body!

explanation.surface: A doctor at breaking point, urged to find a patient or a corpse.
explanation.walkthrough: Police dredge rivers and lakes when searching for a drowned body.
explanation.definitionFit: Dredging a river bed is how a missing body is often searched for.

clue.text: Courting lawyer takes money, quite a bit of money

parts.note: a grand, a thousand pounds or dollars

explanation.surface: A lawyer paid handsomely for courting a client, or a rich partner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Takes' just puts the money after the lawyer; G for grand is a common abbreviation for a thousand.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: courting is the old-fashioned word for going out with someone.

clue.text: Sex just started to get glib for Barney

indicators.note: only the start, the first letter, of sex

parts.note: a pat answer is a glib one

explanation.surface: Someone called Barney smoothly talking his way into bed.
explanation.walkthrough: Barney looks like a name; it is British slang for a row or quarrel.
explanation.definitionFit: A British slang synonym: a barney is a noisy squabble, and so is a spat.

clue.text: Pressure put on press — Russian leader's action?

explanation.surface: Putin cracking down on the media.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests pressure on journalists; the definition points at Stalin's purges, by example, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Russian leaders, Stalin above all, are notorious for purging rivals.

clue.text: Balls twisted on faulty latch — no contest

indicators.note: turned round, so written backwards

parts.note: ED Balls, the politician turned broadcaster

indicators.note: the letters are broken and reordered

explanation.surface: A mishap with a broken lock that ends a match before it starts.
explanation.walkthrough: Ed Balls is a former Labour minister, now a TV presenter. 'No contest' looks like a phrase, but 'no' is fodder and 'contest' the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A decathlon is a ten-event athletics contest.

clue.text: Herb's about, er, to get elected

explanation.surface: A hesitant candidate named Herb who is about to win a seat.
explanation.walkthrough: Herb reads as a man's name; it is the plant. Cumin is really a spice, but the plant is a herb.
explanation.definitionFit: Cumin is a plant of the parsley family, grown for its seeds.

clue.text: Tempt with a kiss and glam wear?

parts.note: X is a kiss at the end of a letter

explanation.surface: Seduction advice: a kiss and something sparkly to wear.
explanation.walkthrough: Lurex is a trade name for a glittery metallic yarn woven into party clothes; the question mark allows for defining a fabric as clothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Lurex is sparkly metallic fabric, the stuff of glam outfits.

clue.text: Alternative fuel must start coming

indicators.note: the start, or first letter, of must

explanation.surface: An energy policy promise: green fuels must be introduced soon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coming' looks like 'on the way', echoing the energy surface; it is the sexual sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A slang sense: 'coming' in the sexual sense means reaching climax.

clue.text: Our nation's anchor — casually dumped in well

indicators.note: dumped in means dropped inside, so the scrambled letters go within the exclamation

parts.note: my! is an exclamation of surprise, like 'well!'

indicators.note: casually means carelessly, so the letters of anchor are jumbled

explanation.surface: The nation's anchor has been carelessly thrown into a well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'casually' scrambles ANCHOR into ONARCH, and 'dumped in' drops it inside MY. The 's of 'nation's' is read as 'is', a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The United Kingdom is a constitutional monarchy, a state headed by a king or queen.

clue.text: Bill's final judgement?

definitions.meaning: a bill in the older sense: an account to be settled
the Last Judgement, when all accounts are settled

explanation.surface: A man named Bill faces his final verdict.
explanation.walkthrough: Bill looks like a name, or a parliamentary bill; it is a bill to pay, an old sense of reckoning.
explanation.definitionFit: A reckoning is an account or bill, and the day of reckoning is the Last Judgement.

clue.text: (& 1ac.) Parrot's gone to meet its maker — early indication of who'll get in?

definitions.text: early indication of who'll get in?

parts.note: a death, a departure from the stage of life
the stock pet name for a parrot, as in 'Pretty ___', in its short form

explanation.surface: Monty Python's dead parrot sketch, retold as election-night news.
explanation.walkthrough: The parrot comes first in the clue but last in the answer: the 's makes it 'Parrot has gone', and the dead bird's exit is written ahead of its name.
explanation.definitionFit: An exit poll, taken as voters leave, is the first sign on election night of who has won a seat.
